_comment: Mutation testing answers the one question the review rounds kept asking by hand: if this guard were removed, would anything notice? Three findings in a row came from deleting a check and watching the suite stay green, and the first full run found three more. Concurrency is cores minus two; four left seven of ten idle.
_runner: Not `npm test`: that also runs test/hygiene.test.mjs, which reads the tracked files looking for real personal data. A mutant in index.js cannot change what is written in a file, so those 10.7 seconds were spent 832 times to learn nothing. The two files left are the ones that drive index.js. If a mutant ever survives that only hygiene would have caught, this line is the reason, and hygiene still runs on every commit.
_incremental: Off, and it has to be. Incremental reuse is decided per mutant from which tests covered and killed it — and the command runner reports the whole suite as ONE synthetic test, whose identity does not change when a test file does. So every mutant looks reusable after any test change, and a run that should have re-checked the new tests reports the old numbers instead. That happened here: an edited config gave an identical 832-NoCoverage summary in twelve seconds. Turning it on again needs coverageAnalysis, which needs a runner that loads the code in-process, which this suite cannot use because it drives the server over stdio as a child.
_timeout: A healthy run of the two files is about 8.5 seconds, and 172 of 832 mutants hang. At the old 60000 those alone were roughly 21 of the 38 minutes — more than every other mutant put together. Stryker's effective limit is timeoutMS plus netTime times 1.5, so 10000 still allows ~23s, near three times a normal run: slack enough that a merely slow mutant is not miscounted as a hang, which would inflate the score rather than deflate it. Concurrency is above the core count on purpose — each runner spends most of its life waiting on a child process and an HTTP fixture, and at 8 the machine sat at half load.
